detail.title: Modern Portfolio Theory in the Crypto-Wilderness

keywords: Applied Computing → Economics Keywords and Phrases Modern Portfolio Theory

detail.abstract: Modern portfolio theory (MPT) prescribes how to maximise the return of an asset portfolio for a given level of risk. The optimal trade-off between return and variance defines the efficient frontier. Whether actual cryptoasset portfolios approximate this prescription and whether proximity to the frontier translates into realised performance remain difficult to test at large scale in traditional markets due to their opaque nature and the inaccessibility of data. As we show, public blockchains make these questions measurable: every token transfer is recorded, thus enabling complete portfolio reconstruction for every account at any point in time. We leverage this transparency to reconstruct cryptoasset portfolios for over 116 M Ethereum accounts across the full chain history (2015-2025), measure their distance to the constrained efficient frontier, and quantify how deviations translate into realised performance. Here we show that market entry timing, not allocation choice, is the dominant predictor of realised cryptoasset returns. On-chain wealth is highly concentrated and portfolios are pervasively under-diversified, with single-asset holdings accounting for 83.35% of accounts. Two-asset portfolios sit closest to the efficient frontier defined by their held assets, a proximity that reflects the narrowness of their opportunity set rather than deliberate optimisation. Passive market-capitalisation weighting outperforms every MPT optimisation strategy in median realised return, and entry month alone explains 70-79% of the variance in returns, far exceeding the contribution of allocation choice. Mean-variance optimisation therefore appears neither descriptive of observed behaviour nor prescriptively useful in the cryptoasset domain, even if MPT retains its value as a normative benchmark.

title: Anger Adaptation Training: How Anger-Currency Environments Transform Workplace Development into Survival-Oriented Behavioral Conditioning
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Anger Adaptation Training: How Anger-Currency Environments Transform Workplace Development into Survival-Oriented Behavioral Conditioning
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the concept of Anger Adaptation Training to distinguish strict workplace training from adaptation to anger. Workplace development is normally expected to improve competence, judgment, reproducibility, safety behavior, and problem-solving capacity. However, in workplaces where anger functions as a form of emotional currency, development may transform into survival-oriented behavioral conditioning. In such anger-currency environments, subordinates do not primarily learn how to perform work better, but how to avoid superiors' anger, read their moods, remain silent, evade responsibility, and sometimes imitate anger toward weaker members.
 Building on the emotional currency model, this paper argues that anger becomes a value medium when it is exchanged for influence, legitimacy, evaluation, and survivability within organizations. When anger is interpreted as strictness, responsibility, seriousness, or result orientation, it may become difficult to distinguish competence development from anger adaptation. The paper therefore distinguishes three forms of training: strict training, which develops ability and judgment; fear resilience training, which develops performance capacity under crisis; and Anger Adaptation Training, which develops survivability within anger-currency environments.
 The paper identifies four major outputs of Anger Adaptation Training: silence adaptation, mood-reading adaptation, responsibility-avoidance adaptation, and mimetic anger adaptation. It also presents a seven-stage model: monetization of anger, learning the predictability of anger, rising speech risk, rationalization of silence and responsibility avoidance, suspension of competence development, emergence of anger imitation, and stabilization of a localized anger ecology. An anonymized building management workplace case is used to illustrate how anger, labeling, public correction, detailed control, silence, and imitation can transform workplace development into survival adaptation.
 The paper concludes that strictness itself is not the problem. The problem arises when strictness becomes embedded in an anger-currency environment and teaches members to survive anger rather than develop competence. Organizational improvement therefore requires not only anger management, but also the redesign of emotional currency environments so that reporting, consultation, dialogue, repair, failure sharing, and laughter remain survivable behaviors.

title:
Stochastic Calculus and Derivatives 
SDEs, Option Pricing, Volatility Models, and Structural Limits of Market Completeness Akmal Xodarev

Stochastic Calculus and Derivatives 
SDEs, Option Pricing, Volatility Models, and Structural Limits of Market Completeness Akmal Xodarev

detail.abstract:
Derivative pricing is treated here as a chain of measurable and martingale reductions. The primitive object is a filtered probability space. Asset dynamics are then specified as adapted stochastic processes with a stated path and martingale status. Trading strategies are admitted only after their measurability, predictability, and self-financing constraints have been fixed. A pricing operator is introduced only after the relevant no-arbitrage and martingale-measure structure has been stated. Under these conventions a derivative price is not a primitive datum; it is the output of a specified mathematical structure.
The first closed benchmark is the Black–Scholes model. Its role is structural. In that model the same Brownian source drives the traded uncertainty and the hedgeable uncertainty; consequently martingale pricing, replication, a parabolic pricing equation, and an explicit formula coincide under the stated assumptions. Once volatility becomes nonconstant, stochastic, path-dependent, incompletely spanned, or empirically unstable, the reductions need not close. The analysis therefore records both positive identities and obstructions: the distinction between physical and pricing measures, the gap between no-arbitrage and uniqueness, the residual created by finite rebalancing, the inverse status of implied volatility, and the non-uniqueness left by calibration. 
The first analytic obstruction is quadratic variation. Continuous finite-variation calculus cannot contain Brownian paths. The stochastic integral is therefore constructed from elementary predictable integrands through an isometry and then extended to square-integrable and local classes. This construction supplies the first martingale market layer: discounted gains become stochastic integrals, admissible wealth is controlled by supermartingale arguments, and unique pricing is tied to attainability rather than to no-arbitrage alone.
The next layer fixes equivalent changes of measure, Brownian drift removal, representation, and Markovian pricing equations. In a full-rank Brownian market, the martingale representation theorem supplies the spanning mechanism and turns conditional valuation into replication. When the volatility matrix loses rank, when the filtration contains untraded noise, or when the pricing function has no classical regularity, the corresponding closure statement is replaced by a diagnostic obstruction.
The stochastic-volatility layer makes the variance process an additional state variable. With one traded stock and two Brownian directions, the martingale-measure condition removes the drift of the discounted stock but leaves an orthogonal measure-change kernel undetermined. Conditional valuation then depends on a volatility-risk selection. A stock-only hedge can project the claim martingale onto the traded direction, but the orthogonal variance component remains as a local martingale residual. Completion requires additional dynamically traded volatility-sensitive assets and a rank condition; vanilla calibration alone is not such a completion.

title: Digital Health Implementation at the Hospital–Residential Aged Care Interface: Evidence, Barriers, and Governance Requirements A Systematic Literature Review, 2000–2025 Dr Marian Sassoli, Dr Geoff Ebbs, Dr Luke Houghton
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Griffith University and Griffith University

detail.title: Digital Health Implementation at the Hospital–Residential Aged Care Interface: Evidence, Barriers, and Governance Requirements A Systematic Literature Review, 2000–2025 Dr Marian Sassoli, Dr Geoff Ebbs, Dr Luke Houghton
detail.abstract: BackgroundAustralia’s aged care sector is undergoing mandated digital transformation, including universal participation in the My Health Record (MHR) infrastructure, under regulatory frameworks introduced following the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety. Yet the evidence that electronic health record (EHR) deployment alone improves patient safety outcomes in residential aged care is strikingly weak — creating an urgent need to understand what enabling conditions effective digital health implementation requires.ObjectivesThis review synthesises evidence on: (1) the nature and extent of medication safety failures at the hospital–residential aged care facility (RACF) transition interface; (2) the barriers, facilitators, and outcomes of digital health technology implementation in aged care; and (3) the workforce, governance, and implementation science conditions that determine whether digital infrastructure produces safe clinical outcomes.MethodsA systematic search of CINAHL, ProQuest, and Scopus, supplemented by snowball sampling, identified 67 peer-reviewed studies (2000–2025). Thematic synthesis across five domains was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, incorporating the MHR Guidelines for Residential Aged Care as a national policy framework.ResultsMedication discrepancies affect up to 75% of RACF admissions following hospital discharge. EHR implementation alone does not reduce discrepancy rates or adverse drug events. Barriers to digital adoption are multi-level, structural, and mutually reinforcing, with only 39.4% of Australian providers using electronic medication management as of 2020. No studies evaluate AI-assisted clinical decision support at the hospital–RACF interface, and all nine digital health implementation studies in the corpus were published between 2020 and 2025.ConclusionsDigital health infrastructure is necessary but insufficient for medication safety improvement. Workforce competency development, implementation science methodology, data governance, and co-design with end users are equally required enabling conditions. The evidence identifies a specific and tractable research agenda for the informatics community.

title: Earning the Right to Govern: Authority Acquisition in Business Analysis Centers of Excellence Through Staged Legitimacy Building

detail.title: Earning the Right to Govern: Authority Acquisition in Business Analysis Centers of Excellence Through Staged Legitimacy Building
detail.abstract: Business analysis centers of excellence (BACoEs) face a governance paradox: they require organizational legitimacy to mandate the standards that generate adoption, yet cannot acquire that legitimacy without the adoption that mandate authority would enable. This study examines how BACoEs resolve this authority dilemma through a mixed-methods design combining a survey of 104 BACoE leaders with longitudinal case analysis of 15 BACoEs over 48 months, drawing on 187 interviews and 458 documents. Three authority governance structures emerged (Directive, Advisory, and Hybrid), producing distinct adoption outcomes by organizational context. Successful BACoEs followed a consistent four-stage legitimacy sequence: cognitive legitimation (months 0–12), normative legitimation (months 12–24), selective regulative legitimation (months 24–36), and institutionalization (months 36+). Political capital was the strongest predictor of adoption outcomes (β = 0.41, p < 0.001), consistently outperforming methodology sophistication and certification levels. This study extends institutional theory to internal service function legitimacy, proposes temporal sequencing as a fourth paradox management strategy, and demonstrates that authority is earned through staged legitimacy building rather than granted through executive charter.

title: Other People's Votes: The Law and Economics of Proxy Advice
affiliations: , Boston College, Carroll School of Management and Georgetown University

detail.title: Other People's Votes: The Law and Economics of Proxy Advice
detail.abstract:
Proxy advisors play a central and controversial role in modern corporate governance. Institutional investors rely on advisory firms such as Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis to provide shareholder voting recommendations, research, and execution infrastructure across thousands of portfolio companies each year, enabling voting at scale. Critics argue that proxy advisors induce “robo-voting,” exercise excessive influence, operate with conflicts of interest, and dominate a concentrated market with limited accountability. In response, federal and state actors have launched an escalating series of investigations, executive actions, and novel statutory and regulatory regimes.

      Many existing reform proposals misdiagnose the economic foundations of proxy advice and risk degrading voting quality or driving proxy advisors from the market altogether. Because institutional investors have limited attention budgets, weakening proxy advisory services would likely increase deference to corporate management rather than enhance shareholder oversight.

      This Article offers an economic framework for evaluating proxy advice and the reforms proposed to regulate it. We develop a three-stage theory of shareholder voting in which investors (1) select proxy advisors, (2) specify customized voting policies ex ante, and (3) allocate scarce attention across proposals ex post. We complement this framework with empirical evidence on voting patterns that reassesses claims of “robo-voting” and advisor dominance. Together, our analysis situates proxy advice within the collective-action problem inherent in shareholder voting: investors bear the concentrated costs of informed voting while capturing only a fraction of its benefits. Building on this analysis, we propose a targeted reform agenda. First, we recommend requiring proxy advisors to provide “attention flags” identifying recommendations that involve material trade-offs, firm-specific context, or high-stakes decisions, thereby directing investor attention to where it is most valuable. Second, we propose strengthening fiduciary obligations governing proxy voting to ensure meaningful engagement where warranted. We also address firm-specific conflicts of interest and evaluate prominent regulatory approaches, including federal solicitation-based regulation and recent state legislation. Our regulatory framework improves the targeting of investor attention while preserving economies of scale, offering a more promising path forward.

title: Network Motifs and the Rise of Entrepreneurial Ecosystems

detail.title: Network Motifs and the Rise of Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial ecosystem research has focused on macro-level configurations, yet the micro-level network structures underpinning ecosystem emergence remain underexplored. I introduce network motif analysis (the study of small recurring subgraphs) to entrepreneurial finance research, examining how emerging patterns in venture capital co-investment networks predict ecosystem rise. Analyzing 29 U.S. state ecosystems from 2015 to 2024, I identify distinct motif signatures for different trajectories. Booming ecosystems display squares and pentagons, i.e. extended trust chains reflecting "friends of friends of friends" logic. Established ecosystems exhibit triangles and hexagons, which are dense, orchestrated structures. Critically, heterogeneous motifs incorporating investors who differ by type, previous success rate, or vintage predict sustained growth more reliably than homogeneous patterns. These findings bridge micro-level network interdependencies with macro-level regional performance, offering policymakers actionable diagnostic tools for catalyzing entrepreneurial growth.

title: Personality Engineering with AI Agents: A New Methodology for Negotiation Research
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Personality Engineering with AI Agents: A New Methodology for Negotiation Research
detail.abstract: According to canonical negotiation theory, people's success in a negotiation depends on how well they balance competing demands--empathizing and asserting, demonstrating concern for other and concern for self, being soft on the people and hard on the problem. Yet people struggle to manage these tensions, so researchers have lacked the ability to rigorously test the field's prescriptions under controlled conditions. AI agents do not face the same limitations, and their precision, repertoire, consistency, and scalability enable a new class of experiments to contribute to negotiation theory. In this article, we introduce personality engineering: a methodology that uses AI agents to precisely parameterize, manipulate, and evaluate negotiator personality. We propose using the interpersonal circumplex--and its two core dimensions of warmth and dominance--as a foundational coordinate system for the field. This approach offers both a rigorous methodology for testing classic negotiation theories and a practical guide for designing the personalities of AI negotiation agents.

title: Impact of Weather Conditions on Cereal Yields in Poland
affiliations: Poznan University of Economics and Business, Poznan University of Economics and Business, Poznan University of Economics and Business, Poznan University of Economics and Business and Poznan University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Impact of Weather Conditions on Cereal Yields in Poland
detail.abstract:
The aim of this study was to assess the impact of weather factors on the yield of selected cereals
in the context of ongoing climate change. The study used variables specifying factors such as temperature, precipitation, as well as control variables, which were the share of medium and heavy
soils in a given province and the consumption of mineral fertilizers in kg of NPK/ha. The dependent
variables were yields of selected cereals. Data were collected from databases of the Polish Institute
of Meteorology and Water Management National Research Institute (IMGW PIB), Poland Statistics
(GUS), and Institute of Soil Science and Plant Cultivation State Research Institute (IUNG PIB).
The meteorological data came from 157 meteorological stations located in 14 provinces. Estimation was carried out for the 2013–2020 period. The study used the panel regression method. For all
the models estimated, there was a significant effect of the number of days with precipitation on yields.
While regularly occurring, moderate rainfall is undoubtedly favorable, large amounts of rainfall can
adversely affect yields. Another statistically significant climatic factor is temperature during spring
and summer, with moderate temperatures being the most favorable for yields. Changes in temperature
affected yield changes in individual cereals with varying intensity, with the strongest effect recorded
for wheat. On the basis of the research carried out, a conclusion was drawn that Polish agriculture will need to adapt to the new conditions by undertaking a number of measures, including changing
the structure of crops, securing the irrigation of plants against possible droughts with efficient, modern irrigation systems, increasing the genetic diversity of plants, and using modern agrotechnics.

title: A Multimodal Explainable AI System for Early Prediction of 30-Day Diabetes Readmission with LLM-Generated Clinical Recommendations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Multimodal Explainable AI System for Early Prediction of 30-Day Diabetes Readmission with LLM-Generated Clinical Recommendations
detail.abstract: Predicting 30-day hospital readmission in diabetic patients is a key challenge in modern healthcare: readmissions within this window signal poor glycaemic management during the index admission and contribute substantially to avoidable costs. Existing machine-learning approaches rely on structured tabular data and often stop short of translating their predictions into actionable guidance for clinicians. We propose a multimodal explainable AI system that addresses both limitations. Using the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (n = 101,766), we augment structured electronic health record (EHR) features with a text modality: feature-conditioned synthetic clinical notes generated by a large language model (LLM) and encoded by Bio+ClinicalBERT into 768-dimensional dense vectors. We compare six models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, a Tabular-Only Neural Network (Tab-NN), an Early Fusion Neural Network (EF-NN), and a Late Fusion Neural Network (LF-NN). A controlled ablation study isolates the contribution of the text modality by comparing EF-NN and Tab-NN, which share identical architecture and training. Our LF-NN achieves AUC-ROC of 0.9067 (95% CI: 0.8827–0.9287), and EF-NN surpasses the architecturally equivalent Tab-NN by +0.2513 AUC-ROC points, confirming that synthetic text embeddings carry complementary predictive signal beyond structured features. Model predictions are explained via SHAP, and a structured LLM-driven recommendation layer translates per-patient feature attributions into natural-language clinical guidance. SHAP analysis identifies prior inpatient admissions, polypharmacy, and glycaemic indicators as the dominant readmission drivers, consistent with established clinical knowledge. Bootstrap confidence intervals confirm that both multimodal models are statistically distinguishable from tabular-only baselines by non-overlapping CIs. Key limitations include the use of risk-label-conditioned synthetic notes, which may carry indirect target-correlated signal, and the small multimodal test subset. Our system demonstrates that combining structured and unstructured data modalities with interpretable AI and natural-language recommendations meaningfully advances both predictive performance and clinical utility.

detail.abstract: Livestock production accounts for 14.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, but many policies rely on information campaigns, assuming that increased awareness will reduce meat demand. Using 2015-2016 survey data from South Africa (n=561) and Norway (n=561), we assessed whether knowledge of the climate impact of meat predicts consumption. Negative binomial regression controlling for demographics showed no significant link between environmental knowledge and meat intake in either country (IRRs ~0.99; p > 0.60). This result was consistent across all models. However, gender is a key predictor: men in South Africa eat approximately 8% more meat than women (IRR=1.08; p=0.04), with similar trends in Norway. The lack of association between knowledge and consumption in two different food systems-one with rising livestock demand and increasing awareness, and the other with established sustainability policies-indicates behavioral barriers to diet change via information alone. These results suggest that policies to cut livestock emissions require structural measures (such as procurement standards, choice architecture, and fiscal tools with safeguards) instead of just consumer education. The gender findings also show that demand policies should address the symbolic link between meat and masculinity.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-To develop a Maqasid-grounded methodology for non-financial performance measurement of Shariah-compliant investments, extending the established operationalization literature in Islamic finance through a framework designed to operate above the eligibility layer of conventional compliance and differentiate among investments that pass screening. Design/methodology/approach-The paper synthesizes the classical Maqasid jurisprudence of Al-Ghazali, Al-Shatibi, and Ibn Ashur with the contemporary scholarship of Siddiqi, Chapra, Kamali, and Auda; reviews the operationalization literature on Maqasid measurement in Islamic finance; and develops the Shariah Alignment Framework-Maqasid (SHAF-M) as a methodological response to the structural gaps identified.

Design/methodology/approach — The paper synthesizes the classical Maqasid jurisprudence of Al-Ghazali, Al-Shatibi, and Ibn Ashur with the contemporary scholarship of Siddiqi, Chapra, Kamali, and Auda; reviews the operationalization literature on Maqasid measurement in Islamic finance; and develops the Shariah Alignment Framework — Maqasid (SHAF-M) as a methodological response to the structural gaps identified.

Findings — The prior literature has established Maqasid measurement as operationally tractable but has not produced a framework with the structural features the next phase of Islamic capital allocation appears to require: external anchoring at every pillar against narrative manipulation, governing doctrine for cross-analyst consistency, framework controls for evidence and inferential discipline, asymmetric hard constraints enforcing substantive over formal coherence, and an explicit two-layer architecture distinguishing eligibility determination from positive-alignment differentiation.

Practical implications — SHAF-M is designed to support portfolio construction within compliant universes where conventional analysis produces undifferentiated outputs; due diligence on individual investments where coherence signals warrant systematic surfacing; and limited-partner reporting where Maqasid alignment can be presented alongside financial reporting as a defensible institutional view.

Originality/value — The paper provides a systematic synthesis of classical and contemporary Maqasid scholarship into an operational methodology, advancing prior operationalization efforts through four methodological moves not previously systematized and through an explicit architectural distinction between Layer 0 (eligibility) and Layer 1 (positive-alignment differentiation).

title: You Can't Tax the Past Without Pricing the Present: The Hidden Costs of Climate Superfund Laws
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: You Can't Tax the Past Without Pricing the Present: The Hidden Costs of Climate Superfund Laws
detail.abstract:
State climate change superfund laws aim to retrospectively tax producers of fossil fuels to defray the costs associated with climate change.  Supporters of these laws suggest that companies like ExxonMobil and Chevron are responsible for the damage caused by the emissions generated when their products are extracted, processed, and ultimately used by end consumers.  Following the “polluter pays” principle, advocates of the laws assert producers should pay the associated costs that come with remediation and mitigation of climate change harms.

 

Fearing backlash from consumers, politicians have been quick to insist that these backward-looking surcharges will not affect the prices people will face for fossil fuel products.  They argue that because the fines will be levied as a fixed amount based on past production and sales, marginal cost is unchanged, leaving current prices unaffected.  Instead, they argue, the costs will come from the ample profits of the oil and gas industry, falling on shareholders, not consumers.

 

There are a number of problems with these arguments.  First, while the fines are retrospective, they set a clear precedent that production will inevitably entail costs in the future.  Those expected costs do constitute a current increase in marginal cost, leading prices to go up today.  Second, given how widely oil and gas industry stocks are held (including in most public pensions funds), the portion of the costs borne by shareholders will fall not just on modern-day Rockefellers but also on teachers, garbagemen, cops, and fire fighters.

 

Further, even the widely invoked “polluter pays” principle is a poor fit in the context of state climate change superfund laws.  A large part of the principle’s motivation is the desire to build external costs into the supply and demand curves faced by decisionmakers in a market.  By ensuring that all social costs are internalized, buyers and sellers face the right incentives leading them to make value maximizing choices.  However, as suggested, supporters disclaim the idea that costs will be internalized.  This precludes the main efficiency benefit of the polluter pays principle.  If producers do prospectively incorporate future fines, as foreshadowed by the current state superfund laws, the polluter pays principle could be back on track.  That said, given the way emissions are allocated to producers in current models, there is no mechanism to encourage producers to engage in pollution-minimizing extraction and production methods, nor is there any incentive for consumers to favor emission-minimizing suppliers.  Current climate change attribution models make little allowance for anything other than quantity decisions by suppliers.

 

Indeed, the existing attribution models primarily allocate emissions to the end-use (i.e., burning) of fossil fuels, which highlights a normative or fairness problem with the use of the polluter pays principle in the context of the state superfund laws.  The motivation used by the laws’ advocates paint producers as the cause of emissions when the attribution models themselves indicate that consumption is the primary cause of the emissions at the root of climate change. 

 

Furthermore, returning to the potential efficacy of the laws in terms of reducing emissions, most economic models suggest that individual firm supply responses have little effect on overall production, as other firms offset marginal reductions of a given firm.  Demand side effects, however, can have a durable effect on overall output.  From both fairness and efficiency perspectives, focusing primarily on producers seems misguided.

title: The Full Pareto Frontier as Kantian Equilibria
affiliations: and Higher Colleges of Technology

detail.title: The Full Pareto Frontier as Kantian Equilibria
detail.abstract: Multiplicative Kantian equilibrium explains cooperative behavior in social dilemmas without abandoning methodological individualism. However, its outcomes depend critically on the parametrization of the strategy space-the property of strategic nonequivalence. We investigate what fraction of the Pareto frontier can be attained by varying the strategy space. We show that the set of achievable Kantian equilibria is the entire Pareto frontier: for any interior Pareto-efficient point there exists a shift of coordinates-imposing lower bounds on actions-that makes it a Multiplicative Kantian equilibrium. The proof is constructive and relies on a intuitive geometric property: moving the origin to a point on the common tangent to players' indifference curves. This result separates the problem of efficiency from the problem of fairness, allowing any normative criterion to be implemented without loss of Pareto optimality.

title: High-volume Plaintiff-side Counsel and Single-appearance Eviction Cases in Philadelphia
affiliations: and University of Pennsylvania,

detail.title: High-volume Plaintiff-side Counsel and Single-appearance Eviction Cases in Philadelphia
detail.abstract: Among 755,004 Philadelphia landlord-tenant records filed during 1969-2022, 396,163 residential cases involve tenants who appear exactly once in the observed docket. In unadjusted comparisons, single-appearance cases handled by high-volume plaintiff-side counsel are more likely to advance to the writ-of-possession and served-writ stages, but no more likely to end in default. Comparisons within the same plaintiff, and within the same plaintiff at the same property, show no broad premium on adverse case outcomes such as default, judgment, or fees. The clearer pattern is organizational: after a plaintiff adopts or switches into high-volume counsel, monthly filings rise by about 2-5% and the number of distinct buildings reached rises by a similar margin; near the prior-year top-10 attorney threshold, cases display local differences in default and enforcement; and continuances under specialist counsel are more closely linked to default. Non-flat pre-treatment trends and imprecise reverse-direction estimates from attorney exits restrict the strength of any causal claim. High-volume plaintiff-side counsel therefore functions as a mechanism of filing scale and procedural sequence, not as a uniform escalator of case outcomes or as a cause of any individual tenant becoming single-appearance.

title: Contractibility Regimes: A Structural Theory of Regulatory Architecture for Future-State Markets

detail.title: Contractibility Regimes: A Structural Theory of Regulatory Architecture for Future-State Markets

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and structural-institutional analysis using only publicly available information (regulatory documents, court filings, published research, public market data). No human subjects research was conducted.

detail.abstract: In 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on prediction markets, asking how event contracts should be treated under public-interest review, gaming restrictions, inside-information rules, manipulation standards, and contract-type classification (Commodity Futures Trading Commission, 2026b). Existing commentary treats these as separate doctrinal problems. This paper develops a common primitive vocabulary for them. The diagnostic move is to treat event contracts not as financial instruments that incidentally produce signals, nor as signals that are incidentally financialized, but as hybrid institutions whose financialized mechanism and publicly consumed price signal are co-constitutive. The framework developed here is organized around that hybridity rather than around financial substrate alone. Novel financial substrates routinely outrun the regulatory categories built for prior asset classes. This paper develops a structural theory of contractibility regimes: institutions that convert uncertain future states into priced, settleable, and publicly usable claims. Rather than analogizing a new substrate to insurance, securities, commodities, gambling, or benchmark administration, the paper decomposes inherited regimes into primitive protection and hazard mechanisms and recomposes the protection bundle appropriate to the new substrate. Event-contract markets are the live specimen because they approximate the minimum binary-settlement contractibility regime over externally resolvable propositions. The framework evaluates contractibility regimes on two axes. The first is stability: whether a regime supplies protection primitives sufficient to dominate the hazards it generates. Stability is represented by an ordinal conservation condition, P(R) ≥ H(R), over primitives including insurable interest, disclosure, solvency/collateralization, admissibility, surveillance, certifier integration, trade reporting, wagering incentive, endogeneity, information asymmetry, externalities, and quote authority. The second is yield: whether contractibilizing a future state produces hedge-completion, observability, or coordination value not already supplied by substitute instruments or institutions. Stability determines whether a contract class can be governed. Yield determines whether building the architecture is worth doing. The paper models event-contract platforms as the candidate free object, or minimum element, in the binary-settlement sub-lattice of contractibility regimes. Adjacent regimes appear as quotients by additional protection relations. The framework is made auditable through a mechanism-derived primitive matrix, a three-pole certifier architecture (de jure, de facto, and cryptoeconomic), a level-distributed unit of analysis, a dynamic drift model, and dated forward predictions. FEDDECISION contracts illustrate a frontier-stable case held together by high admissibility and high de facto certifier integration. Senate-vote contracts illustrate a hard case dominated by endogeneity, certifier externalization, information asymmetry, and quote-authority hazards. Carbon-offset markets illustrate portability beyond event contracts. The central contribution is methodological: regulatory architecture for future-state markets should be derived from invariant contractibility problems, not inherited by analogy from regimes built for prior substrates.

detail.abstract: Across eight prior papers in the WHEEL portfolio, the same diagnostic posture has been operating on different surfaces: organizational readiness, behavior change, agentic governance, regulatory compliance, human-AI collaboration, governance platform architecture, governance layering, and token economics. Each paper appeared to address a different object. In retrospect, each was applying the same method to a different surface of the same underlying problem. This paper names the method: constraint-based diagnostic architecture. A methodology for identifying the binding constraint or binding set in a multi-variable system, measuring how that constraint is experienced across organizational levels, and pointing to what should be addressed first. The methodology operates through structured diagnostic measurement of organizational variables, not through aggregation of respondent opinion. The paper makes three contributions in one architecture. It names the Accountability Layer, the layer of enterprise AI infrastructure that produces diagnosis of what is preventing accountable value from being created, distinct from the capability, observation, and compliance layers that produce descriptions of system state. It articulates the methodology that operates at the Accountability Layer explicitly, by definition rather than by demonstration. And it applies the methodology to enterprise AI accountability, where it produces an inversion: the question is not only whether the workforce is ready for AI, but whether the AI deployment is ready for the workforce it enters. The contribution is bounded. The methodology is not offered as a fully validated field instrument. It is offered as a methodology grounded in established literatures, demonstrated across the portfolio, computationally stress-tested for internal coherence, and specified at sufficient granularity to be tested, falsified, or refined. The portfolio demonstration is offered as evidence of methodological coherence and portability across surfaces, not as independent empirical validation. What this paper provides is the keystone the portfolio has been building toward: the name, the definition, and the operating logic of the method that has been making the hidden constraint visible across eight different surfaces of the AI accountability problem.

title: From Reactive to Proactive: Governance by Design as a Foundational Principle for Responsible AI

detail.title: From Reactive to Proactive: Governance by Design as a Foundational Principle for Responsible AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no funding and was conducted independently. No personal or financial relationships with any organization influenced this work.

detail.abstract: Current AI governance frameworks are reactive by architecture. They detect and respond to failures after they occur rather than preventing them at the point of design. This paper argues that reactive governance is structurally insufficient for AI systems with high human and societal impact, and proposes Governance by Design as an alternative paradigm. Drawing on established principles from software engineering, fault-tolerant system design, and privacy-by-design frameworks, this paper demonstrates how ethical constraints, bias thresholds, and corrective mechanisms can be embedded directly into data pipelines, learning processes, and deployment infrastructure. When governance is built into the system rather than applied on top of it, compliance becomes an inherent system property rather than an external enforcement requirement. Three concrete implementation domains are examined: governing data sources, governing the learning process, and governing deployment and monitoring. The paper concludes that proactive governance transforms ethical alignment from a corrective process into a foundational design principle-and that systems not governed by design will ultimately fail by design.
